items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: 20% of people own 80% of the wealth — and 4% own 64%
items.claim: Vilfredo Pareto observed in 1896 that ~20% of Italians owned ~80% of the land. The pattern recurs in income, book sales, software bugs, city sizes, earthquake magnitudes. Apply 80/20 again to that 20%: 4% own 64%. And again: 0.8% own 51.2%.
items.prompt: Why is this 'fractal' inequality so common?

options.text: Many natural and social processes follow POWER LAWS: P(X > x) is proportional to x to some negative power. Power-law distributions exhibit self-similarity at all scales, including the recursive 80/20 split
It is true only for exactly 20%

items.reveal:
A power-law distribution: the probability that a quantity exceeds x is proportional to x^(-alpha), for some exponent alpha. The Pareto distribution is the canonical example.

When alpha is in a particular range (specifically when the exponent gives an 80/20 split), the distribution is 'self-similar': the top 20% has 80% of the total; within that top 20%, the top 20% (i.e., the top 4%) holds 80% of THEIR share (i.e., 64% of the whole).

Key examples:
- US household wealth: top 20% own ~85%; top 1% own ~32%.
- Earthquakes: each unit increase in magnitude is ~10x less frequent.
- City sizes (Zipf's law, also power law).
- Web site visits, book sales, file sizes, software bug counts.
- Word frequencies in language (Zipf).

Generative mechanisms: 'rich-get-richer' (preferential attachment, scale-free networks — Barabási, Albert 1999); multiplicative growth; minimax processes.

Power laws contrast with normal distributions (bell curves) where extreme values are vanishingly rare. In power-law distributions, extreme values dominate — and you can't reason about averages as 'typical'.
items.why: Equality intuitions assume bell curves. Many real distributions are power laws — where the top few items dwarf the rest, and inequality is built into the math.

items.title: A walker who halves their distance forever still reaches the wall
items.claim: Walk halfway to a wall. Then half of what's left. Then half again. Infinitely many steps — but the total distance is finite (the original distance), and the total time (if you halve your time at each step too) is also finite. Zeno's paradox resolved.

options.text: Infinity — there are infinitely many terms
Exactly 1. Geometric series with ratio r where |r| < 1 sums to a/(1-r); here a = 1/2 and r = 1/2, so sum = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1
Depends on how many terms you take

items.reveal:
A geometric series: a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... For |r| < 1, the sum is a/(1-r).

Proof: let S = a + ar + ar^2 + ... Then rS = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... = S - a. So S - rS = a, giving S = a/(1-r).

Examples:
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = (1/2)/(1 - 1/2) = 1.
0.999... = 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... = 0.9/(1 - 0.1) = 1.
1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... = 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2.

For |r| >= 1: the series diverges. 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... grows without bound.

Zeno's paradoxes resolved: Achilles catches the tortoise in finite time because the catching-up steps form a convergent series. Modern calculus formalises 'limit' and 'sum to infinity', tools Zeno did not have.

Applications:
- Compound interest formulas (sum of payment streams).
- Mortgage/loan calculations.
- Probability of getting heads eventually in repeated coin tosses.
- Resonance in physics (geometric series of wave reflections).
- Convergence of decimal expansions, power series, Taylor expansions.

Fermat, Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy, Weierstrass — the theory of convergent series was refined over centuries. By Weierstrass's epsilon-delta formalisation (1850s), 'infinite sum equals 1' had precise rigorous meaning.

Non-convergent series: harmonic 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges (slowly, but to infinity). Conditional convergence (alternating series) raises subtle issues — Riemann showed you can rearrange a conditionally convergent series to sum to any value.
items.why: Infinite tasks seem impossible. They're not: infinite quantities can sum to finite values, given the right conditions. Calculus tamed Zeno's paradoxes and made motion mathematically describable.
